concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: This is the sole research target, including its mechanism, modes, completion conditions, and failure cases.

concepts.name: SQLite write-ahead logging
concepts.reason: The broader journaling mechanism supplies context but exceeds the requested checkpointing scope.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpointing
concepts.reason: Its thresholds, execution context, and callback configuration determine when checkpoints run.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE
concepts.reason: Its progress and waiting rules define the default checkpoint behavior.

concepts.name: Checkpoint progress
concepts.reason: Reader constraints, saved progress, and starvation explain incomplete checkpoints.

concepts.name: WAL recycling
concepts.reason: The conditions for reusing the WAL are distinct from transferring its contents.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL
concepts.reason: Its waiting conditions clarify when all log frames can be checkpointed.

concepts.name: Large-transaction checkpoint constraints
concepts.reason: Large transactions expose a reset boundary and the packet's dated WAL-growth change.

concepts.name: Checkpoint synchronization
concepts.reason: Synchronization order and configuration are part of the checkpoint mechanism.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART
concepts.reason: Its additional reader wait distinguishes completing frame transfer from enabling log reuse.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE
concepts.reason: Its successful-return behavior provides an explicit truncation variant.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP
concepts.reason: It separates checkpoint status queries from frame-transfer work.

concepts.name: Checkpoint locks and busy handling
concepts.reason: Contention and busy-handler refusal expose blocking, partial progress, and error behavior.

concepts.name: Checkpoint progress counters
concepts.reason: Counter semantics determine how callers interpret reported checkpoint progress.

concepts.name: Checkpoint database selection
concepts.reason: Database selection changes the scope and result semantics of a checkpoint call.

claims.text: SQLite WAL checkpointing moves WAL transactions back into the database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: A new connection's default automatic-checkpoint threshold is 1000 pages or the value of SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() or by automatic checkpointing use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop when it reaches a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: Checkpointing normally leaves the WAL file untruncated, with journal_size_limit identified as an exception.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set).

claims.text: By default, the COMMIT thread executes the automatic checkpoint it triggers.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits for no database writer and for all readers to use the most recent database snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: The WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.
claims.quote: which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.

claims.text: Checkpointing beyond a reader's end mark could overwrite database content that the reader is actively using.
claims.quote: The checkpoint has to stop at that point because otherwise it might overwrite part of the database file that the reader is actively using.

claims.text: The wal-index records checkpoint progress so the next invocation resumes where the previous checkpoint stopped.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before checkpointing moves its content into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: After its waiting conditions are met, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL checkpoints every frame in the log.
claims.quote: It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: Pending SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART checkpoints block new database writer attempts.
claims.quote: Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts while it is pending, but does not impede readers.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART adds to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL a wait after checkpointing until all readers use only the database file.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE extends SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART by truncating the log file to zero bytes immediately before a successful return.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers a checkpoint after a transaction commits if the WAL contains N or more frames.
claims.quote: The sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) is a wrapper around sqlite3_wal_hook() that causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing N <= 0 to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() disables automatic checkpoints entirely.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: A writer rewinds the WAL when its entire contents have been transferred into the database and synced, and no readers still use the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: If overlapping readers keep using the WAL continuously, checkpoint starvation can let the WAL grow without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP accesses *pnLog and *pnCkpt without checkpointing any frames.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: If another process's checkpoint prevents acquiring the checkpoint lock, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: S2 specifies that SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART do not impede readers while pending.
claims.quote: Like SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, this mode blocks new database writer attempts while it is pending, but does not impede readers.

claims.text: In WAL mode with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: Registering a callback through sqlite3_wal_hook() disables automatic checkpointing previously configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: The frame count reported through *pnCkpt includes frames checkpointed before the current call.
claims.quote: If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART, and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE fall back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior if the busy handler returns 0 before obtaining the writer lock or while waiting for readers.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: When busy-handler refusal makes checkpointing continue in SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE style, sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: The callback installed by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() replaces any existing sqlite3_wal_hook() callback.
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .

claims.text: Passing NULL or an empty string as zDb makes sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() attempt the operation on all WAL databases attached to the connection.
claims.quote: If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db.

claims.text: When the operation targets all attached WAL databases, the values written through *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.
claims.quote: the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: Selecting a named attached database outside WAL mode returns SQLITE_OK and sets the supplied *pnLog and *pnCkpt outputs to -1.
claims.quote: If database zDb is the name of an attached database that is not in WAL mode, SQLITE_OK is returned and both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.

claims.text: Older SQLite versions could write the same page into the WAL multiple times when a transaction exceeded the page cache.
claims.quote: However, with older versions of SQLite, the same page might be written into the WAL file multiple times if the transaction grows larger than the page cache.

claims.text: As of SQLite 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), pages changed by a transaction should be written into the WAL only once.
claims.quote: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself. Pages that are changed by the transaction should only be written into the WAL file once.

handoffs.name: SQLite WAL reading
handoffs.reason: Reader page lookup and shared-memory indexing deserve separate research beyond their constraints on checkpoint progress.

handoffs.name: SQLite WAL writing
handoffs.reason: Commit-record creation and general writer serialization are separate operations beyond their checkpoint consequences.

limitations: The frozen packet contains SQLite documentation excerpts, without implementation code, experiments, or independent expert sources; it establishes no independent expert disagreement.

S1 warns that SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE may block readers, while S2 says RESTART does not impede readers and defines TRUNCATE as extending RESTART; the packet does not reconcile this wording.
S1 says manual RESTART/TRUNCATE checkpoints ensure completion, while S2 permits busy-handler refusal, partial checkpoint work, and SQLITE_BUSY; unconditional completion is not established.
S1 enumerates three checkpoint subtypes and refers to RESET, while S2 specifies five SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_* modes; no dated revisions establish a historical sequence between these descriptions.
Historical depth is limited to S1's SQLite 3.11.0 large-transaction change; checkpoint origins, mode-introduction dates, and broader changes in understanding are not supplied.
The three-pass deepening cap was reached with 8/36 new information in pass 3; neither of the final two passes was below 5%, so saturation is not demonstrated.
The 36-claim cap leaves supplied S2 error-propagation and counter cases unenumerated; at least one additional pass could examine them, but the number of passes needed for saturation is unknown.
